verse.text: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen ones, temporary residents of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
verse.note: The word describes someone staying for a time in a place that is not their home, a visiting foreigner without local citizenship. ‘Exiles’, used by several modern translations, suggests banishment, which the Greek does not say; ‘sojourners’ is accurate but no longer current English. Verse 17 uses a related term for living as a resident foreigner. Whether the label describes the readers’ actual social status, their spiritual situation, or both is debated.

This was the established term, taken from the Greek Old Testament, for Jews living scattered among the nations outside the land of Israel. The letter applies Israel’s vocabulary to its readers, many of whom appear from later verses to have been Gentiles.

verse.text: according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through being made holy by the Spirit, for obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you.
verse.note: The pairing of obedience with sprinkled blood recalls the covenant ceremony of Exodus 24, where the people pledged obedience and Moses sprinkled them with the blood of the sacrifice. Most interpreters see that scene behind the phrase, so that the readers are pictured as brought into a covenant through the death of Jesus.

verse.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in his great mercy gave us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in the heavens for you,
who are being guarded by God’s power through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.
In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if it must be, you have been grieved by various trials,
verse.note: The Greek relative can mean ‘in this’ (the whole situation just described), ‘in which’ (the last time, making the rejoicing future), or ‘in whom’ (God or Christ). The verb form can also be read as a command, ‘rejoice’. Most translations take it as a statement referring to what precedes, as here.

verse.text: so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes yet is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
Though you have not seen him, you love him; though you do not see him now, you believe in him and rejoice with a joy that is beyond words and filled with glory,
as you receive the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
verse.note: The Greek word covers life, the self, and the inner person; it does not by itself imply an immaterial part separable from the body. Many scholars think that in this letter it means the whole person, so that the phrase could be rendered ‘the salvation of your lives’ or simply ‘your salvation’. The traditional word is kept here and in verse 22.

verse.text: Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace meant for you inquired and searched carefully,
searching for what time or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ within them was pointing to when testifying in advance to the sufferings destined for Christ and the glories that would follow.

note.term: what time or what kind of time

verse.note: The Greek can be read either as two questions about the time (‘what time or what sort of time’) or as one about a person and one about the time (‘what person or what time’). Several major translations take the second view. Many grammarians and commentators prefer the first, since both question words most naturally attach to the single noun ‘time’, and it is followed here.

verse.text: It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you in these things, which have now been announced to you through those who brought you the good news by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven—things into which angels long to look.
Therefore, with your minds belted for action and staying sober, set your hope fully on the grace being brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.

note.term: with your minds belted for action
note.traditional: gird up the loins of your mind / prepare your minds for action

verse.note: The Greek says literally ‘having girded up the loins of your mind’. People wearing long robes tucked them into a belt before working, running, or travelling, so the expression means getting ready for exertion. It may echo the instruction to eat the Passover with loins girded, ready to leave Egypt.

The adverb stands between ‘being sober’ and ‘set your hope’ and could belong to either: ‘being completely sober, set your hope’ or ‘being sober, set your hope completely’. Most translations take it with ‘hope’, as here, though some commentators argue for the other reading because this author usually places such adverbs after the verb they modify.

verse.text: As children of obedience, do not conform to the desires you had before, in your ignorance,
but, as the one who called you is holy, be holy yourselves in your whole way of life,
for it is written, “You shall be holy, because I am holy.”
And if you call on as Father the one who judges impartially according to each person’s work, live the time of your stay as foreigners in fear,
knowing that it was not with perishable things, silver or gold, that you were ransomed from the futile way of life handed down from your ancestors,
verse.note: The verb means to set free by paying a price, and was used of buying slaves or captives out of bondage; in the Greek Old Testament it describes God freeing Israel from Egypt. ‘Redeemed’ is the older English rendering, but it has become a general religious term and no longer conveys the payment that the mention of silver and gold presupposes. Several modern translations also use ‘ransomed’.

verse.text: but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
He was foreknown before the foundation of the world, but was made manifest at the end of the times for the sake of you
who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.
Now that you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth, leading to sincere love for your brothers and sisters, love one another earnestly from the heart,
verse.note: Many manuscripts read ‘from a pure heart’, and a number of translations follow them. The edition translated here reads simply ‘from the heart’, judging that ‘pure’ was added by copyists. The evidence is fairly evenly divided and editors disagree.

verse.text: since you have been given new birth, not from perishable seed but from imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.

note.term: the living and enduring word of God
note.traditional: the living and abiding word of God

verse.note: Grammatically ‘living and enduring’ could describe either the word or God (‘the word of the living and enduring God’). Most interpreters attach the adjectives to the word, because the quotation that follows says that the word of the Lord endures.

verse.text: For “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls,

note.term: “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls,

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 40:6–8 in a form close to the ancient Greek translation. ‘Flesh’ here means humanity in its frailty and mortality. In Isaiah the passage announces comfort to exiles, which fits the letter’s picture of its readers as foreigners away from home.

verse.text: but the word of the Lord endures forever.” And this is the word that was proclaimed to you as good news.
So put away all malice and all deceit, hypocrisy and envy and all slander,
and, like newborn babies, crave the pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up into salvation,

note.traditional: spiritual milk; milk of the word

verse.note: The adjective normally means 'rational' or 'belonging to the mind', and in religious writing of the period it marks something as non-literal: this is not physical milk. Many translations and commentators instead render 'milk of the word', because the adjective is related to the noun 'word' (logos) and the preceding verses have just spoken of God's word. Both readings are well supported. A different Greek word lies behind 'spiritual' in verse 5.

verse.text: if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.
As you come to him, a living stone, rejected by people but chosen and honored in God’s sight,
verse.note: The word means 'held in honor, highly valued' and is usually rendered 'precious' here and in verse 6. 'Honored' is used so that the reader can hear the link in verse 7, where the related noun 'honor' is applied to those who believe, in contrast to the shame mentioned at the end of verse 6.

verse.text: you yourselves also, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek form can be either a statement ('you are being built') or a command ('let yourselves be built'). Most translations and commentators take it as a statement, as here, but some prefer the command.

verse.text: For it stands in Scripture: “See, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and honored, and whoever believes in him will never be put to shame.”
So the honor is for you who believe; but for those who do not believe, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,”
and “a stone to stumble on and a rock to trip over.” They stumble because they disobey the word, and to this they were also appointed.
verse.note: The Greek noun refers to something that causes a person to fall, a trap or obstacle, not to something that hurts feelings, as 'offense' now suggests. The line comes from Isaiah 8:14; the two quotations before it are from Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22.

verse.text: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, so that you may proclaim the mighty acts of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
verse.note: The word translated 'nation' here is the same word translated 'Gentiles' in verse 12; in the plural it commonly means the non-Jewish peoples. The titles in this verse are drawn from Exodus 19:5–6 and Isaiah 43:20–21, where they describe Israel, and verse 10 echoes Hosea 1–2.

The word usually means 'excellence' or 'virtue', but in the plural and used of a deity it referred to displays of divine power. Peter is echoing the Greek version of Isaiah 43:21, where the word stands for a Hebrew term meaning 'praise', so 'praises' and 'excellencies' are also defensible and widely used.

verse.text: Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
Beloved, I urge you as foreigners and temporary residents to keep away from the desires of the flesh, which wage war against the soul.

note.traditional: strangers and pilgrims; sojourners and exiles

verse.note: The first term was used for a non-citizen living in a place with limited rights, the second for someone staying only for a time. 'Pilgrims' and 'exiles' suggest a religious journey or banishment, which neither word implies. The pair echoes Abraham's description of himself in Genesis 23:4. Scholars debate whether Peter is describing the readers' actual civic status, their social estrangement as Christians, or both.

verse.text: Keep your conduct among the Gentiles good, so that, where they slander you as wrongdoers, they may observe your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.
verse.note: In the Greek Scriptures God's 'visitation' is his coming to inspect and act, whether to rescue or to judge; the phrase occurs in Isaiah 10:3. Whether Peter means the final judgment or the moment when God brings these observers to faith is disputed.

verse.text: Submit, for the Lord’s sake, to every human creature: whether to the emperor as supreme,

note.traditional: every human institution; every ordinance of man

verse.note: Most translations render 'every human institution' or 'authority'. Elsewhere in the New Testament, however, this noun always refers to creation or a created being, and the sense 'institution' is hard to parallel; a number of commentators therefore read 'every human creature', with emperor and governors as the first examples. The question remains open. 'Emperor' translates the ordinary word for 'king', which Greek speakers in the eastern provinces used for the Roman emperor.

verse.text: or to governors as those sent by him to punish wrongdoers and to praise those who do good.
For this is God’s will: that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people.
Live as free people, yet not using your freedom as a cover for evil, but as slaves of God.
verse.note: The word means a slave, a person owned by another, not a hired servant. The paradox is deliberate: those who are free belong wholly to God. In verse 18 'household slaves' translates a different word, used for slaves attached to a household and traditionally rendered 'servants'.

verse.text: Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.
Household slaves, submit to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and considerate but also to the unjust.
verse.note: Many translations have 'with all respect', taking the attitude as directed toward the masters. In this letter, though, fear is owed to God (as in verse 17) and readers are told not to fear human opponents (3:14), so reverence toward God is probably meant. The Greek does not state the object.

verse.text: For this wins favor: if someone, out of awareness of God, bears up under pain while suffering unjustly.

note.traditional: is commendable; is a gracious thing; is thankworthy

verse.note: The word is the one usually translated 'grace'. Here and in verse 20 it is taken in its everyday sense of favor or credit: such conduct is what God looks on with approval. Some interpreters instead read 'this is grace', meaning that such endurance is evidence of God's grace at work.

verse.text: For what credit is there if you sin and are beaten for it and endure? But if you do good and suffer for it and endure, this wins favor with God.
For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you would follow in his footsteps.
He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.
When he was insulted, he did not insult in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness. By his wounds you were healed.
verse.note: The Greek word means wood or something made of wood, such as a beam, stake or gallows, and is used here for the cross. 'Tree' is kept because the wording echoes Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where a body hung 'on a tree' is under God's curse. Verses 22–25 draw throughout on the language of Isaiah 53.

verse.text: For you were like sheep going astray, but now you have turned back to the shepherd and overseer of your souls.
In the same way, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some of them disobey the word, they may be won over without a word through their wives' conduct,
when they have observed your pure and reverent conduct.
verse.note: The Greek says the conduct is ‘in fear’. Most interpreters take this as reverence toward God, in line with the letter's usage elsewhere, and that reading is followed here and in verse 16. Some take it as respect toward the husband.

verse.text: Your adornment should not be the outward one of braiding hair, wearing gold jewelry, or putting on clothes,
verse.note: The Greek has only ‘putting on of garments’, with no word for ‘fine’ or ‘expensive’. Many translations add the adjective because the point is plainly about display, not about dressing at all. The plain wording is kept here, and the context supplies the sense.

verse.text: but the hidden person of the heart, with what is imperishable: a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great value in God's sight.
verse.note: The traditional ‘meek’ now suggests weakness, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone who is not self-assertive or harsh. ‘Gentle’ or ‘humble’ is the usual modern rendering, and the related noun in verse 16 is translated ‘gentleness’.

verse.text: For this is how the holy women of the past who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, being subject to their own husbands,
as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You have become her children, doing good and not fearing anything that terrifies.
verse.note: The reference is to Genesis 18:12, where Sarah speaks of Abraham as ‘my lord’. The word was an ordinary term of respect for a husband or master, much like ‘sir’, and does not imply divinity here. The closing words about fearing nothing that terrifies echo Proverbs 3:25.

verse.text: Husbands, in the same way, live with your wives with understanding, showing honor to the woman as to a weaker vessel, since they are also fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verse.note: ‘Vessel’ was a common image for a human being as a body or creature, and the comparative ‘weaker’ implies that the husband is a vessel too. Most interpreters take the weakness as physical strength or social vulnerability, not moral or intellectual inferiority; the verse goes on to call wives fellow heirs. Some translations paraphrase as ‘weaker partner’ or ‘weaker sex’.

verse.text: Finally, all of you: be of one mind, sympathetic, loving toward one another as brothers and sisters, tender-hearted, humble in mind,
not repaying evil for evil or insult for insult, but on the contrary blessing, because you were called to this, so that you might inherit a blessing.
For “whoever wants to love life and see good days must keep the tongue from evil and the lips from speaking deceit,

text.q: must turn away from evil and do good, must seek peace and pursue it;
for the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears are open to their plea, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

verse.note: Verses 10–12 quote Psalm 34:12–16 in a form close to the Greek Septuagint. Greek has a single word-family where English has two: ‘righteous’ and ‘just’, ‘righteousness’ and ‘justice’. The same family appears in ‘righteousness’ (verse 14) and ‘the righteous for the unrighteous’ (verse 18).

verse.text: And who is going to harm you if you become zealous for what is good?
But even if you should suffer because of righteousness, you are blessed. Have no fear of them, and do not be troubled,

note.traditional: be not afraid of their terror

verse.note: Literally ‘do not fear their fear’, borrowed from Isaiah 8:12, where it means ‘do not fear what they fear’. In this letter's setting most interpreters take it as ‘do not be afraid of them’, meaning the opponents, and that is followed here. The Isaiah sense remains possible, and some translations adopt it.

verse.text: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always ready to give a defense to anyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you,

note.term: honor Christ the Lord as holy

verse.note: The wording continues the allusion to Isaiah 8:13, ‘regard the Lord as holy’, and applies it to Christ. Later manuscripts read ‘the Lord God’, which the King James Version follows; the earliest witnesses read ‘Christ’. The phrase can also be construed as ‘honor Christ as Lord’.

verse.text: yet with gentleness and reverence, keeping a good conscience, so that when you are slandered, those who disparage your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame.
For it is better to suffer for doing good, if the will of God should so will, than for doing evil.
For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring you to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
verse.note: Many early manuscripts read ‘died’ in place of ‘suffered’, and some read ‘bring us’ in place of ‘bring you’. ‘Suffered’ fits the letter's running theme and is the reading of the Greek text translated here, but the choice is disputed.

‘Flesh’ and ‘spirit’ are set in parallel with no preposition in Greek. Most scholars take them as two spheres or modes of existence: Christ was put to death as a mortal human and made alive in the realm of the spirit, that is, in resurrection. Others read the second as ‘by the Spirit’, naming the Holy Spirit as agent.

verse.text: in which he also went and made proclamation to the spirits in prison,
verse.note: This is one of the most disputed verses in the New Testament. Many modern scholars identify the spirits as the rebellious angelic beings of Genesis 6, whom Jewish tradition such as 1 Enoch describes as imprisoned, with the risen Christ announcing his victory to them. Others take them as the human dead of Noah's generation, or hold that Christ preached through Noah to people then living. The verb means only ‘announce as a herald’ and does not state what was proclaimed.

verse.text: who had once disobeyed, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah while an ark was being built, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were saved through water.
Baptism, the counterpart of this, now saves you too—not as the removal of dirt from the flesh but as the pledge of a good conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,

note.term: the pledge of a good conscience toward God
note.traditional: the answer of a good conscience toward God

verse.note: The Greek noun is rare, and its meaning here is disputed. In contracts of the period it is used for a formal undertaking, which supports ‘pledge’. The related verb means ‘ask’, which supports ‘an appeal to God for a good conscience’, the choice of several major translations. Either way, the contrast is between washing the outside and an inward commitment directed to God.

verse.text: who has gone into heaven and is at God's right hand, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to him.
Since Christ, then, suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same way of thinking, because whoever has suffered in the flesh has finished with sin,

note.term: whoever has suffered in the flesh has finished with sin
note.traditional: he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin

verse.note: The clause is compact and disputed. It may describe the believer who, by accepting suffering, has made a decisive break with sin; it may refer to Christ himself; or it may echo the idea that one who has died with Christ in baptism is freed from sin. The opening word can also mean ‘that’ instead of ‘because’, making the clause the content of the ‘way of thinking’. The rendering leaves these options open as far as English allows.

verse.text: so as to live the rest of your time in the flesh no longer by human desires but by the will of God.
For the time already past was enough for doing what the Gentiles choose to do, living in debauchery, desires, drunkenness, revels, drinking parties, and forbidden idolatries.
verse.note: The Greek word means ‘peoples’ or ‘nations’ and, in the plural, was the ordinary Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples; English uses both ‘Gentiles’ and ‘nations’ for this one word. The readers of this letter appear to have been largely non-Jews themselves, so the term here marks the pagan society they have left, not their ancestry.

verse.text: They think it strange now that you do not rush with them into the same flood of reckless living, and so they slander you.
But they will give an account to the one who stands ready to judge the living and the dead.
For this is why the good news was announced to the dead as well: so that, though judged in the flesh by human standards, they might live in the spirit by God's standard.
verse.note: Most current scholars take ‘the dead’ to be believers who heard the good news while alive and have since died: condemned in human eyes, they will nevertheless live before God. Others connect the verse with 3:19 and understand a proclamation to the dead in the underworld, and an older view takes ‘dead’ to mean spiritually dead. The Greek does not settle the question, and ‘in the spirit’ could also be read as ‘by the Spirit’.

verse.text: The end of all things has come near. So keep a sound mind and stay sober for the sake of your prayers.
Above all, keep your love for one another constant, because love covers a multitude of sins.

note.term: love covers a multitude of sins

verse.note: This echoes Proverbs 10:12 in a form closer to the Hebrew text than to the Greek Septuagint, and the same saying appears in James 5:20. It seems to have circulated as a proverb among early Christians. Whether the sins covered are those of the one loved or of the one who loves is not stated.

verse.text: Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each of you has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of the varied grace of God.

If anyone speaks, let it be as one speaking God's own words; if anyone serves, as one serving by the strength that God supplies, so that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a saying of divine origin and is used in the Septuagint for words spoken by God. ‘Oracles’ is the traditional rendering and is accurate, but it suggests pagan shrines to many modern readers. The point is that anyone who speaks in the community should do so as one delivering what comes from God.

verse.text: Dear friends, do not think it strange that a fiery ordeal has come among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you.
verse.note: The word means a burning and was used of the smelting furnace in which metal is refined and proved genuine. The letter has already used this picture in 1:7, where faith is tested like gold in fire. The suffering is thus presented as a test that proves, not as mere destruction.

verse.text: Rather, to the degree that you share in the sufferings of Christ, rejoice, so that at the revelation of his glory you may also rejoice and exult.
If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.

note.term: the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you
note.traditional: the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified

verse.note: Later manuscripts add a sentence at the end of this verse (‘on their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified’), which is why it appears in the King James Version. Some manuscripts also read ‘the Spirit of glory and of power and of God’. The edition translated here, with most modern editions, regards both as additions. The wording echoes Isaiah 11:2.

verse.text: Let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or a wrongdoer, or as a meddler in other people's affairs.

note.term: a meddler in other people's affairs
note.traditional: a busybody in other men's matters

verse.note: This word is not found in any earlier Greek text and may have been coined by the author; it combines ‘belonging to another’ with ‘overseer’. Most scholars take it to mean someone who interferes in matters that are not their concern. Other proposals include an embezzler of property held in trust or a political agitator. The meaning remains uncertain.

verse.text: But if anyone suffers as a Christian, they should not be ashamed, but should glorify God in this name.
verse.note: The word occurs only three times in the New Testament (also Acts 11:26 and 26:28). It is formed in the Latin manner to mean a partisan or adherent of Christ. It was probably coined by outsiders, perhaps as a term of contempt. Here it appears as a label under which believers may be accused, and the letter tells them to bear it as an honour.

verse.text: For the time has come for judgment to begin with the house of God; and if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who disobey the good news of God?
verse.note: The Greek word means both a building and a household. It may refer to the community as God's household, or, following 2:5 where believers are a ‘spiritual house’, as God's temple. The idea of judgment beginning at God's sanctuary echoes Ezekiel 9:6. ‘House’ is kept because it can carry either sense.

verse.text: And “if the righteous person is barely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?”

note.term: “if the righteous person is barely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?”

verse.note: This quotes Proverbs 11:31 almost word for word in its Greek (Septuagint) form. That form differs from the Hebrew, which speaks of the righteous being repaid on earth. ‘Barely’ means ‘with difficulty’: it does not cast doubt on the outcome but points to the hardship through which the righteous are brought.

verse.text: So then, let those who suffer according to the will of God entrust their lives to a faithful Creator as they do good.
verse.note: The Greek word covers a person's life and self as well as the inner person, and with a verb of entrusting it means handing oneself over for safekeeping. ‘Souls’ is the traditional rendering, but it may suggest to a modern reader an immaterial part distinct from the person. Many modern translations render ‘entrust themselves’.

verse.text: So I urge the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a sharer in the glory that is about to be revealed:
shepherd the flock of God that is among you, watching over it not under compulsion but willingly, as God would have it; not for shameful gain but eagerly;
verse.note: The Greek participle behind this phrase is missing from some important early manuscripts, including the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus; it is retained here because the edition translated prints it. The verb is related to the noun for 'overseer' (traditionally 'bishop'), so the elders are described as doing an overseer's work. The phrase 'as God would have it' is also absent from some manuscripts.

verse.text: not lording it over those allotted to you, but becoming examples to the flock.

note.traditional: those entrusted to you; those in your charge

verse.note: The Greek word means a lot or an allotted portion, and is plural here: the 'portions' are most naturally the groups of believers assigned to each elder's care. The King James rendering 'God's heritage' supplies 'God's', which is not in the Greek. In the Septuagint the word is used for Israel's allotted shares of land, and for Israel as God's own portion.

verse.text: And when the chief shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading wreath of glory.
verse.note: The Greek word normally denotes a wreath of leaves or flowers awarded to victorious athletes and to people publicly honoured, not a monarch's crown, for which Greek had another word. The adjective 'unfading' depends on that picture: ordinary wreaths wither, this one does not. Most English versions keep 'crown'; lexicons recognise the wreath as the primary sense.

verse.text: In the same way, you who are younger, submit to the elders. And all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

note.traditional: be subject to the elders; submit to your elders

verse.note: The same Greek word means both 'older men' and 'elders' as holders of a role in the community. Since verses 1–4 address elders as leaders, that sense is kept here, but paired with 'you who are younger' the word could simply mean older people. Interpreters are divided, and some think both ideas overlap.

The verb is rare and means to tie or fasten a garment on oneself. A related noun appears to have referred to an apron or overgarment tied on by slaves and workers, so the image may be of putting on a servant's dress; the evidence is thin, and this association is probable rather than certain.

note.term: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

verse.note: This quotes Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek (Septuagint) form, with 'God' in place of the Septuagint's 'the Lord'. The same line is quoted in James 4:6. The words 'humility', 'humble' and 'humble yourselves' in verses 5–6 all share one Greek root, and the repetition is deliberate.

verse.text: Humble yourselves, then, under the mighty hand of God, so that he may lift you up at the right time,
throwing all your anxiety onto him, because he cares about you.
Stay sober; stay awake. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, looking for someone to devour.
verse.note: The word for 'adversary' is primarily a legal term for one's opponent in a lawsuit, though it was also used more broadly for an enemy. 'Devil' translates a Greek word meaning 'slanderer' or 'accuser', which the Septuagint uses for the Hebrew 'satan'. A first-century reader may therefore have heard a courtroom accuser behind the image of the prowling lion.

verse.text: Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being endured by your brotherhood throughout the world.
And the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself, after you have suffered a little while, restore, steady, strengthen and ground you.
To him belongs the power forever and ever. Amen.

note.traditional: To him be the power (or dominion)

verse.note: The Greek has no verb, so the sentence can be a wish ('to him be the power') or a statement ('to him belongs the power'). The statement is chosen here because the parallel doxology in 4:11 has an explicit 'is'. Most English versions translate it as a wish.

verse.text: Through Silvanus, the faithful brother, as I regard him, I have written to you briefly, urging you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.

note.traditional: By Silvanus; with the help of Silvanus

verse.note: The phrase can mean that Silvanus carried the letter to its recipients, or that he helped write it as secretary or co-author. Comparable expressions in ancient letters usually identify the bearer, and many scholars now favour that reading, but the secretary view is long established and remains possible. Silvanus is generally identified with the Silas of Acts, Paul's companion.

verse.text: She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son.

note.term: She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you
note.traditional: She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen; the church that is at Babylon

verse.note: The Greek has only a feminine adjective, 'the co-chosen one', with no noun. Most interpreters take this to be the congregation from which the letter is sent, since the Greek word for 'church' is feminine; some older versions add 'church' to the text. 'Babylon' is widely understood as a coded name for Rome, as in Revelation and other Jewish writings of the period, though a literal Babylon has occasionally been proposed.

verse.text: Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
